refuted.exploitation: No exploitation path exists from this header alone. A Report-Only CSP is, by spec, never an enforcement point: the browser parses it and posts/logs violations without blocking. Turning it into `Content-Security-Policy` would not block script injection either, because the policy it carries is `script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline' 'unsafe-eval'` (next.config.ts:45) — inline and eval'd script are explicitly permitted. The only directive with real blocking value that the app does not otherwise have (`frame-ancestors 'none'`, next.config.ts:59) is already delivered enforcing by `X-Frame-Options: DENY` (next.config.ts:28) in the same array. Reaching any harm requires a separate, unrelated XSS/HTML-injection bug; nothing in this file creates one.
refuted.rationale: Reachable in production (next.config.ts:137-160 applies SECURITY_HEADERS to `/:path*`), and unconditional — the report-only key is a literal, no env var or flag gates it, so step 2 cannot refute it. Refuted at step 3: the value is not a security control the application relies on being disabled, it is an un-adopted defense-in-depth layer. The Skip-when clause 'read but never consulted at the enforcement point' applies literally here — Report-Only is definitionally non-consulted. The controls in the same array that do enforce (HSTS next.config.ts:24-26, nosniff :27, X-Frame-Options DENY :28, Referrer-Policy :29, Permissions-Policy :35-36) already cover clickjacking, MIME sniffing and transport, and the report-only policy's own `'unsafe-inline' 'unsafe-eval'` (next.config.ts:45) means flipping the key would add no meaningful XSS mitigation. No authentication, authorization, signing, encryption or credential decision in this codebase consults it. Worth noting as hardening, not as a fail-open defect.

refuted.exploitation: No user who could gain anything can reach the null-role state. `profiles.account_role` is enum-typed and `SET NOT NULL` (supabase/migrations/017_account_sharing.sql:122 and :275), and `profiles` has `UNIQUE(user_id)` (supabase/migrations/001_initial_schema.sql:22), so `maybeSingle()` cannot error on duplicates and any existing profile row yields a value `isAccountRole()` accepts. A client cannot blank or change it: the `enforce_profile_privilege_columns` trigger raises `insufficient_privilege` on any UPDATE of `account_role` from the `authenticated` role (supabase/migrations/034_fix_profiles_update_rls.sql:58-81). So an agent or viewer — the roles the nav_* keys actually restrict — always resolves to a real role and is gated at middleware.ts:106. The only population hitting the fail-open is a session with no profile row at all, and that session is locked out everywhere that matters: `getCurrentAccount()` throws ForbiddenError for it (crm/src/lib/auth/account.ts:133-137), which every dashboard API route funnels through via `requireRole`, and the RLS predicate `can_view_by_assignment` requires a matching `profiles` row to return true (supabase/migrations/041_granular_permissions.sql, `can_view_by_assignment` body). Such a user gets an empty page shell, no data and no writes.
refuted.rationale: Reachable in production (middleware runs on the matcher at middleware.ts:125-129) and unconditional — `role` is runtime data, not configuration, so step 2 cannot refute it. Refuted at step 3: the skipped check is a navigation/URL gate whose data-level counterparts fail closed for exactly the same unresolved-profile state. The comment's own framing is accurate but the gap is not a privilege boundary: `canAccessPath` already fails closed on null via `effRole()` (nav.ts:97-99, 114), and the middleware simply never calls it for profile-less sessions, whose authorization is denied downstream by account.ts:133-137 and by RLS (041). Every role that the nav_* keys are designed to restrict is NOT NULL-constrained and client-immutable, so the fail-open branch is unreachable to them. Defense-in-depth divergence, not an exploitable bypass.

refuted.sink: none — value terminates at crm/src/app/api/account/invitations/route.ts:245 as a display string in the response body
refuted.exploitation: The unconfigured permissive branch is real (route.ts:90 returns true when ALLOWED_INVITE_HOSTS is absent, so getBaseUrl trusts X-Forwarded-Host at route.ts:107 or Host at route.ts:112), but the derived string never reaches a security decision. Its single consumer is `inviteUrl(token, getBaseUrl(request))` at route.ts:245, which does pure string concatenation (crm/src/lib/auth/invitations.ts:70-73) into the 201 JSON body. The token is generated independently at route.ts:217 by `generateInviteToken()` (invitations.ts:46-49) and stored only as a SHA-256 hash at route.ts:223; redemption validates that hash server-side, so the base URL affects neither issuance, scope, expiry nor acceptance. For the phishing scenario to work an attacker must control the headers of the victim admin's request, which is not possible: the endpoint is gated by `requireRole("admin")` at route.ts:169, `Host` is a forbidden header name for fetch/XHR, and an injected `X-Forwarded-Host` makes the request non-simple, so a cross-site attempt is stopped by the CORS preflight (the route sets no CORS headers). An attacker who can set the headers is issuing the POST themselves, meaning they are already an admin of that account and already receive the plaintext token in the same response — no privilege or information gain.
refuted.rationale: Steps 1-3 all pass: the route ships in production, the candidate is configurable and boots permissive when ALLOWED_INVITE_HOSTS is unset (route.ts:77-83, :90), and that unconfigured state is the less-secure one. Refuted at step 4: traced to its only sink, the value is a cosmetic base URL echoed to the authenticated admin who made the request; it is never consulted for authentication, authorization, token validation, redirect, or transport verification. deployment_supplies_var is `never` — no manifest sets ALLOWED_INVITE_HOSTS (checked Dockerfile, docker-compose.yml, .github/workflows/ci.yml, .github/workflows/migrations.yml; only NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL is plumbed, at Dockerfile:27,31 and docker-compose.yml:13, and it is itself optional) — but per step 5 that moves severity only and does not resurrect a candidate with no security sink.

refuted.exploitation: Not exploitable. No account member can reach the null-role branch: profiles.account_role is a Postgres ENUM (supabase/migrations/017_account_sharing.sql:53 creates account_role_enum with exactly owner/admin/agent/viewer) declared NOT NULL (017_account_sharing.sql:122 adds the column, :275 applies SET NOT NULL), so isAccountRole(rawRole) (src/lib/auth/roles.ts:54-59) is always true for any existing row and the gate at src/middleware.ts:106 always runs. profiles_select (017_account_sharing.sql:612) is `auth.uid() = user_id OR is_account_member(account_id)`, so a user can always read their own row — RLS cannot suppress it. The only reachable path to role=null is profile being absent entirely, which happens only when the signup trigger swallows an error (017_account_sharing.sql:679-682, EXCEPTION WHEN OTHERS ... RETURN NEW) — i.e. a user with no account membership at all, who gains nothing: the same account_role gates the data in the database (can_view_by_assignment, 040_rls_agent_assignment_visibility.sql:53-55, matches neither the owner/admin/viewer IN-list nor 'agent' when no profiles row exists, so every SELECT returns empty; is_account_member, 017:144-164, likewise) and every API route via getCurrentAccount, which throws ForbiddenError('Profile is not linked to an account') at src/lib/auth/account.ts:133-137 and ForbiddenError('Unknown account role') at :139-143 for exactly the case the middleware lets through.
refuted.rationale: Refuted at step 3: the insecure state is unreachable for anyone who could escalate with it, and where reachable it is gated by an outer authorization layer at the same trust boundary (the corpus 'Skip when' line). The candidate's premise — that isAccountRole returns false for 'a NULL column, a future enum value, or a manually-inserted profile row' — does not hold against the schema: the column is a NOT NULL enum (017_account_sharing.sql:122 + :275), so an agent or viewer can never present an unrecognized value and never bypasses canAccessPath. The single reachable case (no profiles row at all, possible only via the swallowed exception at 017_account_sharing.sql:681) yields a user who renders empty page shells: the identical role field enforces the real boundary in RLS (040_rls_agent_assignment_visibility.sql:53-55) and in every route guard (src/lib/auth/account.ts:133-143). The middleware gate is, per its own comment (src/middleware.ts:87-92) and nav.ts:101-115, a navigation gate against a typed URL or bookmark, not the data boundary — which is why nav.ts effRole() can default to 'agent' for the UI while this layer defers. The asymmetry with nav.ts:97-99 is a hardening opportunity (making middleware.ts:106 read `!canAccessPath(role, ...)` and let effRole fail closed costs nothing), not a grant of access to a party who should not have it.

refuted.exploitation: Not exploitable. The derived base URL is consumed at exactly one place, src/app/api/account/invitations/route.ts:245 (`url: inviteUrl(token, getBaseUrl(request))`), inside the 201 response body of a POST gated by requireRole('admin') at :169 — which resolves the caller's role through getCurrentAccount and throws ForbiddenError for agent/viewer (src/lib/auth/account.ts:191-196). The same response body already returns the plaintext token itself at :244, so an admin who spoofs Host learns nothing they did not already receive in the same JSON. The URL is never emailed, never delivered out of band to a victim, and never re-read as an authorization input — inviteUrl is pure string concatenation (src/lib/auth/invitations.ts:70-73). The classic Host-poisoning threat model (a reset link mailed to a third party) has no analogue here: the file's own header (:10-17) states the admin copies the link out of the creation modal and shares it manually. Browser-driven CSRF cannot reach it either, since JS cannot set the Host header.
refuted.rationale: Refuted at step 3: the unconfigured permissive state is real (parseAllowedHosts returns null at :77-83 when ALLOWED_INVITE_HOSTS is unset, isHostAllowed then returns true at :90, and no deploy manifest sets the variable — Dockerfile, docker-compose.yml and both workflows only carry NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL, docker-compose.yml:13 and Dockerfile:27,31 — so deployment_supplies_var is 'never'), but the permissiveness is already gated by an outer authorization layer at the same trust boundary, the corpus 'Skip when' line. Only an authenticated admin of the account (route.ts:169) can invoke the path, and the value they influence is handed back only to them, alongside the very token it would supposedly exfiltrate (route.ts:244-245). No party who should not have the token gains it. The residual is cosmetic — a misconfigured or probed Host yields a broken invite link for the admin who requested it — which is why the code documents it as defense-in-depth (:54-69) rather than a control. Setting ALLOWED_INVITE_HOSTS (or NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL, which short-circuits header trust entirely at :95-96) remains good hygiene.

refuted.exploitation: Not exploitable. Enumerating every call site of requireApiKey in src/ (excluding tests), all sixteen pass an explicit scope except one: src/app/api/v1/me/route.ts:22. Every data-bearing route is covered — messages/route.ts:46 'messages:send', broadcasts/route.ts:48 and broadcasts/[id]/route.ts:19 'broadcasts:send', contacts/route.ts:37,98 and contacts/[id]/route.ts:27,42 'contacts:read'/'contacts:write', conversations/route.ts:25, conversations/[id]/route.ts:20 'conversations:read', conversations/[id]/messages/route.ts:24 'messages:read', webhooks/route.ts:23,51 and webhooks/[id]/route.ts:24,51,125 'webhooks:manage'. The one scope-free route returns only the caller's own identity: account id, account name, key id, and the key's own scope list (me/route.ts:24-27). A key holder already possesses all of that — it is the value they were handed at creation — so no party gains access to anything they should not have. The key still passes full liveness authentication (findActiveKeyByHash, api-context.ts:89-95, covering unknown/revoked/expired) and per-key rate limiting (:99-102) before reaching the omitted check, and the account is pinned at lookup time (:113), so nothing crosses an account boundary.
refuted.rationale: Refuted at step 3: this is the corpus's 'deliberate public endpoint with a stated reason' shape, not a permissive grant. The scope-free behavior is documented at both ends — src/app/api/v1/me/route.ts:2-13 declares it the identity probe that 'requires nothing but a valid key (no scope)', and src/lib/api-keys/scopes.ts:47-52 states that an empty scope list 'yields a key that authenticates but can't do anything beyond the scope-free endpoints (e.g. GET /api/v1/me)'. The behavior is therefore designed and load-bearing: a zero-scope key must be able to verify itself. The candidate's real complaint is ergonomic — that a future call site could forget the second argument — which is a hardening suggestion (make scope required and pass an explicit sentinel for /me), not a defect in the code as it stands. Asking the category's question, 'who gains access', the answer today is: a valid key, to its own identity. That is the SECURE half of the corpus pair, so the finding does not meet the report bar.

refuted.exploitation: Not exploitable in any state a deployment actually serves. The candidate's own concession is correct and verified: supabase/migrations/017_account_sharing.sql:508-509 issues `DROP POLICY IF EXISTS "Service role can insert messages" ON messages` and replaces it with account-scoped policies messages_select (:510-512) and messages_modify (:513-518, both USING and WITH CHECK requiring is_account_member(c.account_id, 'agent')), and 040_rls_agent_assignment_visibility.sql:70-92 tightens them again onto can_view_by_assignment. Migrations are applied as one cumulative set by the installer before the app is started (the project's own rule: applied versions are tracked in supabase_migrations.schema_migrations by number, and no consumer stops at 001), so the permissive window exists only between two statements of an unattended migration run against a brand-new Supabase project — one that has no conversations rows to target as conversation_id and whose anon key has not yet been written into any client. There is no attacker-reachable moment in which WITH CHECK (true) is the live policy on populated customer data.
refuted.rationale: Refuted at step 3: judged as the state that runs, the value is not permissive — the policy does not exist in any fully-migrated instance. I confirm the underlying observation is technically accurate in isolation: the policy carries no TO clause (so it defaults to PUBLIC, reaching anon and authenticated, not only service_role, which bypasses RLS anyway and never needed a policy), and because permissive policies OR together, its WITH CHECK (true) would defeat the paired ownership check that the FOR ALL policy at 001_initial_schema.sql:182-183 contributes to INSERT. But the schema is the cumulative migration set, and 017_account_sharing.sql:508 removes it unconditionally within the same set, so it never governs a serving deployment. The residual is a hypothetical partially-applied database that is already non-functional (later migrations add the account_id columns every query depends on) and not yet reachable by any client. Worth noting for schema hygiene — a policy named for the service role should carry `TO service_role`, and the fix belongs in 001 so no fork can ever stop short of 017 — but it is not a live permissive-access grant.

report:
# Insecure-Defaults Audit — crm-whatsapp-instalador/crm

## 1. Summary

| Severity | Count |
|---|---|
| CRITICAL | 0 |
| HIGH | 0 |
| MEDIUM | 0 |
| LOW | 14 |

All 14 confirmed findings fall under **debug-features**: API routes that return a raw database error (`PostgrestError.message`) or a raw thrown `Error.message` verbatim in the HTTP response body instead of a generic message. The actual exposure is schema/constraint/policy-name disclosure to authenticated callers (in a few cases scoped further to admin or shared-secret holders) — never a credential, a token, or row data. No CRITICAL/HIGH/MEDIUM findings, and no configurable fallback-secret or default-credential findings survived verification.

**All 14 findings are unconditional** — there is no environment variable, flag, or deployment setting that changes this behavior. They are insecure as written, not insecure-if-misconfigured, so remediation is a code fix in each handler, not a deployment/config change. This is the same reason the run found zero configurable findings to report: every fail-open and permissive-access candidate that depended on an unset variable was traced and refuted (see §5) because either the value never reaches a security decision, or an outer authorization layer already gates the same boundary.

## 2. Findings

All findings below are severity **LOW**.

---

### Finding: Raw PostgREST/Postgres error text returned in API error responses
Locations:
- `src/app/api/automations/route.ts:23`

### Finding: Unbounded catch-all forwards thrown `Error.message` instead of a generic message
Locations:
- `src/app/api/whatsapp/templates/[id]/route.ts:226`
- `src/app/api/whatsapp/templates/submit/route.ts:255`
- `src/app/api/whatsapp/templates/sync/route.ts:310`

Pattern (`templates/[id]/route.ts:226`, identical shape in the other two):
```ts
} catch (error) {
    console.error('Error editing template:', error)
    return NextResponse.json(
      { error: error instanceof Error ? error.message : 'Failed to edit template.' },
      { status: 500 },
    )
```

Verification: The catch wraps the whole handler and forwards any thrown `Error.message` verbatim. `submit/route.ts` and `sync/route.ts` special-case `UnauthorizedError`/`ForbiddenError` through `toErrorResponse` first (visible in the extracted code, lines directly above the sink), so only the *generic* branch is affected there; `templates/[id]/route.ts:226` has no such special-case at all — an auth error thrown deeper in the handler would also flatten into this same raw-message 500. Possible messages include JS `TypeError`s naming internal object shape, GCM decrypt failures from `src/lib/whatsapp/encryption.ts`, or raw Meta Graph API error text.

Production Impact: Unconditional — no configuration mitigates any of the three. `toErrorResponse` is one import away and is already used in the same files for the auth-error branch.

Exploitation: `templates/[id]/route.ts:226` is reachable by any signed-in user (this route has no `requireRole`, only `auth.getUser()`); `submit/route.ts:255` and `sync/route.ts:310` require `requireRole('admin')`. In all three cases the disclosed content is schema/provider-error text, not a secret.

## 3. Remediation

All 14 findings share one fix shape and one existing helper:

1. **Route the DB-error branch through `toErrorResponse` (or an equivalent generic-500 helper) instead of `{ error: error.message }`.** Files: `src/app/api/automations/route.ts`, `src/app/api/automations/[id]/route.ts`, `src/app/api/automations/cron/route.ts`, `src/app/api/flows/route.ts`, `src/app/api/flows/[id]/route.ts`, `src/app/api/flows/[id]/activate/route.ts`, `src/app/api/flows/cron/route.ts`, `src/app/api/quick-replies/route.ts`, `src/app/api/quick-replies/[id]/route.ts`. Log `error.message` server-side (several already do, e.g. `flows/cron/route.ts:94`) and return a fixed string (`Internal server error` or a route-appropriate constant) in the body. `src/lib/auth/account.ts:69-75` is the reference implementation already in this codebase.

2. **Close the catch-all gap in the templates routes.** Files: `src/app/api/whatsapp/templates/[id]/route.ts` (lines 211 and 226, plus the noted sibling DELETE branches at 316/325), `src/app/api/whatsapp/templates/submit/route.ts:255`, `src/app/api/whatsapp/templates/sync/route.ts:310`. Two changes: (a) replace the raw-message JSON with a generic message the way `toErrorResponse` does, keeping the useful non-secret advice text (e.g. `Run "Sync from Meta" to recover.`) but dropping the interpolated `${updErr.message}` / `${delErr.message}`; (b) in `templates/[id]/route.ts` specifically, add the `UnauthorizedError`/`ForbiddenError` special-case that `submit` and `sync` already have, so an auth failure thrown mid-handler doesn't get flattened into a 500 with a leaked message.

No secrets manager, startup validator, or env-var change is applicable here — every finding is a code-level response-shaping bug, not a missing/defaulted configuration value.
